claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has low hardness and strength because dislocations nucleate and glide easily.
The CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has high stacking-fault energy.
Solute-dislocation interactions in this alloy are weak.
High stacking-fault energy and weak solute-dislocation interactions activate multiple slip systems.
Easy dislocation glide produces rapid dynamic recovery.
Rapid dynamic recovery limits dislocation accumulation and work hardening.
Limited work hardening leads to low hardness and yield strength.
The starting material is an as-cast, coarse-grained, single-phase disordered CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Combined in situ TEM and micropillar compression can be used to investigate nanoscale deformation mechanisms.
Crystal orientation can be selected to investigate the activation of particular slip systems during micropillar compression.
Room-temperature and 77 K mechanical testing can be used to characterize changes in deformation mechanisms.
The proposed mechanism remains applicable from quasi-static to high strain rates.
Dislocations move along multiple {110} or similar slip systems in the specified CoCrFeNiTi state.
TEM will reveal extensive planar slip with relatively smooth dislocation paths.
TEM will reveal early dynamic recovery and a low tangled-dislocation density.
The base alloy will exhibit lower yield stress and less strain hardening than variants containing engineered obstacles to dislocation motion.
Introducing dispersoids, precipitates, or other obstacles should reduce dislocation mobility and dynamic recovery.
Failure of an obstacle-engineered control to increase yield stress or strain hardening, or to reduce dislocation mobility and recovery, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
